newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Rumours, technicals may send Belgian OLOs tumbling.
newsitem.headline: Rumours, technicals may send Belgian OLOs tumbling.

text.p: Belgian linear bonds have a slender immediate upward potential but could slide in the next few days on a cocktail of technical factors and market rumours -- denied by official sources -- that Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt might quit, traders said.

"There are the technicals, there are rumours Maystadt might resign...we could fall a full point, possibly from tomorrow," one said. The rumours said Maystadt might leave over criticism that positions from currency swaps by a previous government so far threatened a loss to the government of 44 billion francs.
But official sources strongly denied the rumours.

"This is certainly not the case," said one official source on the rumours. Maystadt was already finance minister when the 1989-1992 government made the currency swaps in an effort to cut the state's bulging debts.

Other official sources played down the impact of the rumours, noting that the 10-year yield spread over Bunds, still at 12 basis points at Tuesday's close, had slipped to a record low of five basis points today. It widened to eight again in late trade, unchanged from Wednesday.
One trader said the spread might even go flat over Germany in the next few days.
"Bunds will be hit hardest if and when the sell-off starts," one trader said.
Traders said Thursday's OLO business was almost purely professional with little institutionals active.

The benchmark 2006 OLO finally closed with a yield of 6.09 percent against 6.05 percent on Wednesday. Prices were chopped by Bunds which sank to lows in the afternoon after U.S. weekly jobs data which were above market expectations.
Traders said that buying, especially in the two to five year area by foreign players, could not conceal the fact that the market looked vulnerable.
The benchmark OLO put on a brave face in the morning but cracked in the afternoon, one said.
Despite the gloomy short-term outlook, some dealers were still convinced of a longer-term rise in bond markets to fresh record highs.
One said it was unlikely that the yield spread with Germany would widen considerably during such rise.
